Document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md so CI runs load them.
Add the missing helper functions to the codebase so the generated tests compile exactly as written.

hints: The CI run needs project context, and there is one file it already loads for that.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Every time a developer pushes a new commit, the review job posts its full set of findings again, so an eight-comment issue accumulates across four pushes. Developers have started ignoring the bot. What should the re-run do?
cards.answer: Including the prior findings in context and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues prevents duplicates while keeping feedback continuous. Deleting previous bot comments destroys the discussion threads attached to them. Reviewing only the final commit removes feedback during the work. A collapsed summary hides duplicates behind a fold without removing them.

choices.text: Post findings as a single collapsed summary comment that is rewritten in place on each push.
Only run the review on the final commit, once the developer marks the pull request ready.
Include the prior findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
Delete all previous bot comments before posting the new set on each push.

hints: The re-run has no idea what it already said last push.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Your nightly test generation job proposes scenarios the existing suite already covers, and reviewers spend their morning discarding them. What change most directly reduces the duplication?
cards.answer: Providing the existing test files in context is what lets generation avoid scenarios already covered - the direct fix. Asking for fewer tests reduces volume, not the duplicate rate. Skipping files that already have a test file skips files whose coverage is partial. An instruction not to duplicate asks for awareness the model does not have.

choices.text: Run generation only on files that have no test file next to them at all.
Ask for fewer tests per run so reviewers have a smaller set to sort through.
Add an instruction telling Claude not to write tests that duplicate existing coverage.
Provide the existing test files in context so generation can avoid scenarios already covered.

hints: The model cannot avoid duplicating coverage it has never been shown.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

A pipeline stage has Claude generate a migration script and, in the same session, review that script for correctness. The review consistently approves code that later fails in staging. What explains this and what should change?
cards.answer: A session that just generated the code retains its own generation reasoning and is less likely to question its decisions, so the review belongs in an independent instance without that context. A longer checklist and extended thinking both add effort inside the same biased context. Running the review twice in the same session repeats the same bias and suppresses findings that appear only once.

choices.text: The model needs extended thinking enabled for the review step to catch subtle issues.
The review prompt is too short, so extend it with a longer and more detailed checklist.
The review should run twice in the same session and flag only issues that appear both times.
The session retains its generation reasoning, so run the review in an independent instance without that context.

hints: The reviewer already believes the code is right, because it is the one that wrote it.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Developers say the review bot cries wolf. Its prompt says "report only high-confidence issues and be conservative", yet it still flags naming preferences and local style choices alongside real bugs. What is the most effective revision?
cards.answer: General instructions like "be conservative" or "report only high-confidence issues" do not improve precision; explicit categorical criteria - what to report (bugs, security) versus what to skip (minor style, local patterns) - do. Capping the number of findings truncates a list that is still mostly noise. A numeric confidence score relies on a poorly calibrated self-assessment. Ranking with a second call ranks noise rather than removing it.

choices.text: Keep the wording and require the model to attach a numeric confidence score to each finding.
Keep the wording and lower the number of findings the bot is allowed to post per pull request.
Replace the confidence language with categorical criteria naming what to report and what to skip.
Keep the wording and have a second model call rank findings, posting only the top three.

hints: "Be conservative" is the instruction that already failed. The fix names categories, not confidence.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Findings are split into four categories. Three are accurate, but the performance category is wrong most of the time, and developers have started dismissing all four without reading them. You need to keep improving the performance prompt. What do you do meanwhile?
cards.answer: High false-positive categories undermine confidence in the accurate ones, so temporarily disabling the bad category restores trust while its prompt is improved. A disclaimer leaves the noise in the feed. Requiring two approvals to dismiss adds process friction to a bad signal. Merging it into the security category contaminates one that currently works.

choices.text: Disable the performance category temporarily so the accurate ones regain developer trust.
Merge performance findings into the security category so they inherit its credibility.
Keep posting all four and require two approvals before a performance finding can be dismissed.
Keep posting all four categories and add a note explaining that performance findings are unreliable.

hints: One noisy category is costing you the credibility of the three good ones.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

The same class of issue is labeled critical in one pull request and minor in another. The prompt lists severity names with one-line definitions. How do you get consistent classification?
cards.answer: Defining each severity level with concrete code examples of what belongs in it is what produces consistent classification. Reducing the scale to two levels hides the inconsistency in coarser buckets. Asking for a justification explains a choice without constraining it. A second ranking call adds a second judgment with the same ambiguity.

choices.text: Ask the model to justify each severity choice in a sentence appended to the finding.
Have a second call re-rank the severities after the review pass completes.
Define each severity level with concrete code examples that illustrate what belongs in it.
Reduce the scale to two levels so there is less room for the model to disagree with itself.

hints: One-line definitions leave the boundary to interpretation. Show the boundary instead.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Findings vary in shape: some name a file and line, some describe the issue vaguely, some suggest a fix and some do not. Your prompt already lists the four required elements in detail. What technique most reliably fixes the format?
cards.answer: When detailed instructions alone still produce inconsistent formatting, few-shot examples showing complete findings in the exact target format are the most effective technique. Repeating the four elements at both ends repeats guidance that has already failed. Rejecting and re-requesting is a retry loop over a fixable prompt. Converting the list into a numbered procedure reorganizes prose without demonstrating the target.

choices.text: Convert the instruction list into a numbered procedure the model must follow in order.
Reject and re-request any finding that is missing one of the four elements.
Repeat the four required elements at both the start and the end of the prompt.
Add few-shot examples showing complete findings in the exact target format.

hints: The instructions are already detailed and already failing. Something else is the strongest lever for format.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Your reviewer flags every direct database call inside a request handler, but in your codebase that pattern is acceptable in admin scripts and problematic only in request paths. Listing the exceptions in prose has not worked. What should you add?
cards.answer: Few-shot examples contrasting acceptable occurrences with genuine issues reduce false positives while letting the model generalize the distinction to novel cases. A path rule that excludes anything containing "admin" is a heuristic that misses the actual criterion. "Report only when highly confident" is the vague confidence language that does not work. A snippet-based filter only suppresses what you have already seen.

choices.text: An instruction to report the pattern only when the reviewer is highly confident it is a problem.
A rule excluding any file whose path contains the word admin from this category of finding.
A post-processing filter that drops findings matching a list of known acceptable snippets.
Few-shot examples contrasting acceptable occurrences with genuine issues, so the model generalizes the distinction.

hints: The distinction is real but contextual, and prose has not carried it. Show both sides.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Your manager wants to move two workloads to the Message Batches API for the 50% savings: a blocking pre-merge check developers wait on, and a technical debt report reviewed the next morning. How should you respond?
cards.answer: The Message Batches API gives 50% savings but has a processing window of up to 24 hours and no latency SLA, which fits the overnight report and not a check developers block on. Moving both and polling bets a blocking workflow on typical completion times. Keeping both synchronous over correlation concerns is wrong - `custom_id` correlates responses. A batch-with-synchronous-fallback adds complexity and pays twice for the blocking case.

choices.text: Keep both synchronous, because batch responses cannot be correlated back to their requests.
Move both to batch with a fallback that re-sends synchronously when a batch runs long.
Move the technical debt report to batch and keep the pre-merge check on the synchronous API.
Move both to batch and poll for completion, since batches usually finish well before the limit.

hints: One workload has a person waiting on it; the other is read the next morning.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

A nightly batch of 400 repository analyses returns with 12 requests failed because those repositories exceeded the context limit. The other 388 succeeded. What is the appropriate handling?
cards.answer: `custom_id` identifies the failed requests, so only those twelve are resubmitted, chunked to fit the context limit. Resubmitting the whole batch pays for 388 successful analyses again. Dropping the twelve accepts a gap that is fixable. Retrying them unchanged repeats a deterministic failure - exceeding the context limit is not a load condition.

choices.text: Retry the 12 unchanged, since context limit failures are usually transient under load.
Resubmit only the 12 failed requests, identified by custom_id, after chunking those repositories.
Drop the 12 and report on the 388 that succeeded, noting the coverage gap in the summary.
Resubmit the entire batch after chunking, so every result comes from an identical configuration.

hints: You already know which twelve failed and why. Change only what caused it.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

A pull request touching 14 files gets a single-pass review that is detailed on some files and superficial on others, misses obvious bugs, and flags a pattern in one file while approving identical code in another. How should you restructure it?
cards.answer: Per-file passes for local issues plus a separate cross-file integration pass fix the attention dilution that produces uneven depth and contradictory findings. Requiring developers to split pull requests shifts the burden onto them without improving the system. A larger context window misreads an attention problem as a capacity problem. Three passes with a two-of-three consensus suppresses real bugs that only one pass catches.

choices.text: Analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate pass focused on cross-file data flow.
Require developers to split pull requests into batches of three or four files before review runs.
Move to a model with a larger context window so all 14 files fit comfortably in one pass.
Run three independent passes over the full pull request and report only issues found in at least two.

hints: The uneven depth and the contradictory findings have the same cause, and it is not capacity.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

Your review always covers the same four aspects in the same order: correctness, security, tests, and documentation. Every pull request needs all four, and the steps do not depend on discoveries made along the way. Which decomposition pattern fits?
cards.answer: Prompt chaining fits a predictable multi-aspect review: the four aspects are known in advance and each runs as a focused step. Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended investigation, which this is not. A single prompt covering all four is the undivided pass that dilutes attention. Parallel subagents with no coordinator remove the coordination that keeps findings consistent.

choices.text: Prompt chaining, running the four aspects as a predictable sequence of focused steps.
A single prompt covering all four aspects so the model can weigh them against each other.
Dynamic decomposition, letting each step decide which aspect to examine next.
Parallel subagents with no coordinator, each posting its own findings independently.

hints: Nothing here depends on what an earlier step discovers.

cards.question:
**Scenario 5 - Claude Code for Continuous Integration**

When your job concatenates per-file analyses into one final report request, findings from the middle files are frequently missing from the summary, while the first and last files are always represented. What mitigates this?
cards.answer: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: models reliably process the beginning and end of a long input. Placing a key-findings summary at the start and giving each file's results explicit section headers mitigates it. Sorting by importance accepts the loss for everything after the top. Shortening each analysis reduces size without addressing position. Sending the request twice is a costly workaround with no guarantee.

choices.text: Put a key findings summary at the start of the input and separate each file's results under explicit headers.
Sort the files so the most important ones are always first, accepting that the later ones may be dropped.
Send the aggregation request twice and merge whatever findings differ between the two responses.
Shorten every per-file analysis so the whole aggregate fits in a smaller portion of the window.

hints: The position of the content in the input is doing the damage.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your extractor asks Claude to "return a JSON object with these fields" and about one response in twenty fails to parse: a trailing comma, a code fence, or a field renamed. What is the most reliable way to guarantee schema-compliant output?
cards.answer: Defining an extraction tool whose input schema *is* your JSON schema, and reading the structured `tool_use` response, is the documented way to eliminate JSON syntax errors, because the structure is enforced rather than requested. A lenient parser repairs symptoms and can silently accept the wrong shape. Lower temperature reduces variance without removing it. Retrying pays for repeated calls to solve a fixable problem.

choices.text: Ask for JSON and repair the malformed responses with a lenient parser before validating them.
Define an extraction tool whose input schema is your JSON schema and read the structured tool_use response.
Ask for JSON and retry the request whenever the response fails to parse on the first attempt.
Ask for JSON and lower the temperature so the model is more consistent about formatting.

hints: Stop asking for JSON. Make the structure something the model fills in rather than writes.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your invoice schema marks purchase_order_number as required. Many invoices simply do not carry one, and in those cases the model produces plausible-looking numbers that do not exist. What is the correct schema change?
cards.answer: Making the field optional or nullable lets the model report absence instead of inventing a value - a required field pressures it to produce something plausible. Instructing it to write "N/A" encodes a sentinel inside a typed field. Validating against the purchase order system afterwards detects the fabrication instead of preventing it. A separate boolean keeps the fabricated value and adds a flag next to it.

choices.text: Keep it required and add a separate boolean field indicating whether the number was actually present.
Keep it required and validate the extracted number against the purchase order system afterwards.
Keep it required and instruct the model in the prompt to write "N/A" when the number is missing.
Make the field optional or nullable so the model can report its absence instead of inventing a value.

hints: A required field the document does not have is a hallucination machine.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your document_type enum lists invoice, receipt, purchase_order, and contract. Roughly 8% of incoming documents are none of these, and the model forces them into the closest match. Which schema design handles this best?
cards.answer: An `"other"` enum value paired with a detail string keeps the vocabulary closed for downstream consumers while remaining extensible for cases you did not enumerate. Adding every observed type is a chase that never ends. Free text loses the constrained vocabulary consumers depend on. Routing unmatched documents to a human sends away work the schema could absorb.

choices.text: Keep the enum and route documents that do not match any value to a human before extraction.
Add an "other" enum value paired with a detail string that captures the actual document type.
Remove the enum and let the field accept any free-text document type the model chooses.
Add every additional document type observed so far as its own enum value.

hints: Downstream consumers still need a closed vocabulary, and 8% of documents will not fit it.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Incoming documents may be an invoice, a shipping manifest, or a warranty claim, each with its own extraction tool, and the type is not known before processing. You need a structured result every time, never a conversational reply. How do you configure tool_choice?
cards.answer: `tool_choice: "any"` requires the model to call a tool while leaving the choice of schema to it, which is what an unknown document type needs. `"auto"` still allows a plain text response. Forcing the invoice tool applies the wrong schema to two of the three types. Passing only the invoice tool discards the other schemas you already built.

choices.text: Force the invoice tool, which covers the largest share of the incoming documents.
Set tool_choice to "auto", since the model will call a tool whenever a document is present.
Set tool_choice to "any", requiring a tool call while letting the model pick the matching schema.
Set tool_choice to "any" and pass only the invoice tool, converting other types afterwards.

hints: You need a guaranteed tool call, but you must not name which one.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your pipeline must always run extract_metadata before any enrichment tool, because the enrichment steps depend on the document date and issuer. Occasionally the model skips straight to enrichment. What guarantees the ordering?
cards.answer: Forced tool selection - `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` - names the tool that must be called, and enrichment proceeds in follow-up turns. `"any"` guarantees a call but not which one. Merging metadata extraction into every enrichment tool duplicates the work on every call. A system prompt line is prompt-based ordering with a non-zero failure rate.

choices.text: Merge metadata extraction into every enrichment tool so the data is always available.
Add a system prompt line stating that extract_metadata must always be called first.
Set tool_choice to "any" and describe the required order in each enrichment tool's description.
Force the first turn with tool_choice naming extract_metadata, then handle enrichment in follow-up turns.

hints: The requirement is about *which* tool runs first, not that some tool runs.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

You adopted tool use with a strict JSON schema and syntax errors disappeared. Auditors then found invoices where the line items do not add up to the stated total, and one where the shipping address was placed in the billing field. What does this show?
cards.answer: Strict schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones - line items that do not sum, a value in the wrong field - so semantic validation is a separate layer in code. Expecting the schema to express the arithmetic relationship asks JSON Schema for something it does not do here. Calling it a misconfiguration misattributes a known limit. Blaming the source documents blames them for an extraction error.

choices.text: The documents are malformed and should be rejected before extraction rather than validated after.
The schema is too permissive and should express the arithmetic relationship between the total and the items.
Strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones, so validation must also check meaning.
Tool use was misconfigured, since a correctly configured schema also enforces field semantics.

hints: The schema guaranteed the shape. Nobody ever promised it would guarantee the meaning.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Two extractions fail validation. In the first, the date arrived as "03/04/2026" where the schema requires ISO 8601. In the second, the required contract value appears only in an amendment your pipeline never received. Which will a retry with error feedback fix?
cards.answer: Retry with error feedback fixes format and structural errors, so the date reformats correctly from the same document; it cannot recover information that is absent from the source, so the contract value in a missing amendment will never appear. Saying both is ignoring that limit. Saying neither dismisses a technique that works for format errors. Saying only the contract value assumes the value is hidden rather than missing.

choices.text: The contract value, because a more explicit instruction usually surfaces fields the model overlooked in its first pass.
Neither, because retries repeat the same conditions that produced the failed extraction.
Both, since retrying with the specific validation error lets the model correct either problem.
The date, because it is a format error the model can correct from the same document.

hints: Ask, for each case, whether the answer is somewhere in the document the model was given.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Extraction works well on documents with labeled tables but returns null for required fields when the same data is written into narrative paragraphs, and you have several dozen documents of each style. What improves the handling of the varied formats?
cards.answer: Few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both tabular and narrative layouts are the recommended fix for null or empty extractions caused by structural variety, and they generalize to formats you did not include. A regex classifier plus separate prompts builds a brittle router for a problem the examples solve. Telling the model data may appear in prose restates the goal without demonstrating it. Converting narratives to tables adds a lossy step ahead of the real work.

choices.text: Route each document to a different prompt after classifying its layout with a regular expression.
Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both the tabular and the narrative layouts.
Instruct the model that data may appear in prose and it should search the whole document.
Convert every narrative document into a table before extraction using a separate model call.

hints: The model handles one layout well and the other badly. Show it the second one.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your extraction pipeline reports 97% field-level accuracy overall, and leadership wants to remove human review entirely. What is the necessary check before doing that?
cards.answer: An aggregate accuracy figure can hide a document type or field that performs badly, so breaking it down by segment is the necessary check before removing human review. A bigger sample only sharpens the same aggregate. Stability over three months shows a possibly misleading number is stable. A confidence threshold acts on scores that have not been validated per segment.

choices.text: Break the accuracy down by document type and by field to confirm no segment performs badly.
Increase the validation sample size until the overall accuracy estimate has a much tighter confidence interval.
Set a model confidence threshold high enough that the remaining extractions are reliable.
Confirm the 97% figure is stable across the last three months before changing the process.

hints: 97% overall can be 99% on one document type and 60% on another.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Extractions the model marks high-confidence are auto-approved and never reviewed. You need to know whether that population is drifting or developing new failure modes, without restoring full review. What should you implement?
cards.answer: Stratified random sampling of the auto-approved high-confidence extractions, reviewed on an ongoing basis, is how error rates get measured and novel failure modes get detected in a population you stopped reviewing. Reviewing downstream rejects only sees failures the downstream system already catches. A first-occurrence rule for new templates covers new templates but not drift in familiar ones. A distribution comparison signals change without telling you whether it is an error.

choices.text: A comparison of this month's field value distributions against last month's as a drift alarm.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, reviewed on an ongoing basis.
A monthly review of every extraction the downstream system rejected as invalid.
A rule that any extraction from a new document template is reviewed on its first occurrence.

hints: You need to measure a population that nobody looks at any more.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Reviewer capacity covers about 15% of daily volume, and today that 15% is chosen at random. You want the reviewed subset to contain as many real errors as possible. What is the best routing strategy?
cards.answer: Field-level confidence, calibrated against a labeled validation set, turns a raw score into a usable routing signal, so the lowest-confidence extractions consume the limited reviewer capacity first. Routing by monetary value targets impact but not error likelihood. Using raw scores as produced sets a threshold whose meaning has never been established. Random sampling optimizes for an unbiased error estimate rather than for catching errors.

choices.text: Have the model emit field-level confidence, calibrate thresholds on a labeled set, and route the lowest first.
Route the documents with the largest monetary values, since those errors are the most expensive.
Route whatever the model flags as low confidence, using the raw scores exactly as produced.
Keep random sampling, which gives an unbiased estimate of the true error rate across all of the documents.

hints: A raw confidence score means nothing until something external tells you what the number is worth.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Some source documents contain contradictory values, for example a summary page stating one total and the detail page another. The extractor currently picks one and reports a single number with no indication of the conflict. What should it do?
cards.answer: Returning both values with an explicit conflict flag surfaces the inconsistency and lets the downstream process decide how to reconcile it. Preferring the detail page applies a heuristic that will sometimes be wrong. Returning null discards information the reviewer needs. Picking the value that matches the line items hides a real inconsistency behind a plausible rule.

choices.text: Return both values with a flag marking the conflict, letting the downstream process decide how to reconcile.
Return null for the field so the discrepancy is treated as missing data and reviewed by a human later.
Return the value from the detail page, which is generally more precise than a summary.
Return the value that matches the sum of the line items, discarding the other one silently.

hints: The document disagrees with itself. That fact is data, not noise.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your document store MCP tool returns the same isError response whether the file is missing, the format is unsupported, or the storage service timed out. The agent retries all three the same number of times. What should the tool return instead?
cards.answer: Distinct error categories with an `isRetryable` flag prevent wasted retries on permanent failures while preserving retries for transient ones: a storage timeout is retried, an unsupported format is not. The raw storage exception leaks internals and still leaves the decision ambiguous. One error type with a wait time assumes everything is transient. A successful response with an empty document reports failure as success.

choices.text: A single error type with a suggested wait time, since retries are the only recovery path available.
A successful response containing an empty document, so the agent can continue with the remaining files.
Distinct categories with an isRetryable flag, so a timeout is retried and an unsupported format is not.
The underlying storage exception verbatim, giving the agent the most detailed possible information.

hints: Three failures, three different right responses - and the agent currently cannot tell them apart.

cards.question:
**Scenario 6 - Structured Data Extraction**

Your extraction agent writes accepted records straight into the downstream warehouse through a write_record tool. Compliance requires that records below a confidence threshold never reach the warehouse without human sign-off. Prompt instructions have not been sufficient. What do you implement?
cards.answer: A hook that intercepts `write_record` calls, blocks low-confidence records and routes them to the review queue enforces the compliance rule deterministically and redirects to the correct workflow. A stronger system prompt is the approach that already failed. A nightly cleanup job removes records after the violation happened. Requiring the confidence value in the call records the number without preventing the write.

choices.text: A schema change requiring the model to include the confidence value in every write_record call.
A hook that intercepts write_record calls, blocks low-confidence records, and routes them to the review queue.
A nightly job that scans the warehouse and removes records written below the confidence threshold.
A stronger system prompt that repeats the threshold and the consequences of writing an unreviewed record.

hints: Prompt instructions already failed, and compliance is not a probabilistic requirement.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your loop sends the request, and when the response carries a tool_use block it executes the tool and immediately calls the API again with the original messages array. The agent keeps requesting the same lookup over and over until the iteration cap trips. What is wrong?
cards.answer: Each iteration must append the assistant turn verbatim and then a user turn carrying the tool_result blocks; re-sending the unchanged history means the model never sees the answer and re-asks forever. Raising the cap lets the same loop spin longer. Nothing indicates a malformed payload, and the model never receives it anyway. Telling the agent it already has the information does not put the information in context.

choices.text: The system prompt does not tell the agent that it already has the information it asked for.
The assistant turn and the tool_result are never appended, so every call repeats the same state.
The tool is returning a malformed payload the model cannot interpret, so it asks again.
The iteration cap is too low for a workflow that legitimately needs several lookups in a row.

hints: Read the loop description again: what does it send on the second call that it did not send on the first?

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

A reviewer proposes replacing your stop_reason check with a decision tree: classify the customer's message, then run a fixed tool sequence for that class. Refunds always run get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund in that order. What is the main cost of this change?
cards.answer: Model-driven decision-making lets Claude choose the next tool from what the current context shows; a pre-configured sequence gives that up, so a case that needs a different path cannot get one. MCP tools are reachable either way. Cost is a side issue, not the architectural one. Error handling is perfectly possible inside a fixed sequence - it just cannot change course.

choices.text: The classification step doubles the token cost of every conversation the agent handles.
Fixed sequences make error handling impossible, since no step can report a failure upward.
The agent can no longer adapt its tool calls to what earlier results reveal.
Decision trees cannot call MCP tools, only tools defined directly in the Messages API request.

hints: Ask who decides the next tool in each design, and what happens when the case is not the usual one.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Policy requires that a fraud check runs before any account credit above $200. Engineering added the rule to the system prompt, to the tool description, and to a few-shot example, and it still slips about once every few hundred conversations. Management asks for a guarantee. What do you tell them?
cards.answer: Prompt-based guidance has a non-zero failure rate by nature, and deterministic compliance requires programmatic enforcement that blocks the downstream call until the prerequisite completes. Restating the rule a fourth time repeats an approach that has already failed three times. Temperature changes sampling, not compliance. Accepting the rate is exactly what the request rules out.

choices.text: Add a prerequisite gate in code that blocks the credit tool until the fraud check has returned.
Accept the current rate, because a failure every few hundred conversations is within normal tolerance for a language model.
Add the same instruction to a fourth location, so the rule appears wherever the model is likely to look.
Lower the temperature for these conversations, which makes the model follow instructions more strictly.

hints: Three prompt-level attempts have already been made. The fourth thing is not a prompt.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

An escalation reaches a human agent with this payload: "Customer is upset about a delayed order and wants a refund. I was unable to resolve it." The human has no access to the transcript or the tool results. What is missing?
cards.answer: A structured handoff carries the facts the agent resolved - identity, amounts, root cause, recommendation - because the human cannot see the tool results that produced them. The transcript is what the human is already being spared, and it still would not contain tool output. A confidence score does not help resolve the case. A list of tool names asks the human to redo the agent's work.

choices.text: The list of tools the agent called, so the human can repeat them and see the same results.
A confidence score explaining how certain the agent was that escalation was the right call.
The customer ID, the order and amount in dispute, the root cause found, and a recommended action.
A transcript of the conversation, so the human can read what the customer said in their own words.

hints: The human cannot see anything the tools returned. Everything they need has to be in the payload.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your billing MCP tool returns status as an integer (2 = settled, 3 = disputed) while the orders tool returns status as a lowercase string. The agent regularly tells customers a disputed charge is settled. You want the fix to apply to every conversation without touching either backend. Where does it belong?
cards.answer: A PostToolUse hook transforms heterogeneous tool results deterministically before they enter the model's context, which is the documented pattern for normalizing formats across MCP tools. Descriptions and system prompt tables both leave the translation to the model on every turn. Validating the finished reply catches the error after the customer-facing text exists, and only when the checker can tell.

choices.text: In the system prompt, as a lookup table the agent consults whenever it reports a status to a customer.
In the tool descriptions, which can explain what each numeric code means so the model can translate.
In a validation step after the response is generated, which rejects replies that name the wrong status.
In a PostToolUse hook that maps both representations onto one canonical status before the model reads them.

hints: The fix has to sit between the tool returning and the model reading, and apply on every turn.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

You need two behaviours around process_refund: refunds over $500 must never execute, and every refund result must be enriched with the customer's loyalty tier before the model reasons about it. Which combination is correct?
cards.answer: Blocking an action is a property of the outgoing call, so it belongs in the interception hook; transforming what comes back is a property of the result, so it belongs in PostToolUse. A PostToolUse hook fires after the refund already executed, which is too late to block it. Enrichment cannot happen before the tool returns the data being enriched. A tool description is prompt-level and guarantees nothing.

choices.text: Intercept the outgoing tool call for both, because enrichment must happen before the tool runs.
Use a PostToolUse hook for both, since it is the hook that has access to the refund amount.
Use the tool description for the threshold and a PostToolUse hook for the enrichment.
Intercept the outgoing tool call for the threshold, and use a PostToolUse hook for the enrichment.

hints: One requirement is about a call that must not happen, the other about data that comes back.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your system prompt opens with "You are an escalation-first support agent. Always consider whether a case should be escalated." Since it was added, the agent calls escalate_to_human on routine cases whose tool descriptions clearly cover them. What should you check first?
cards.answer: Keyword-sensitive system prompt wording can create unintended tool associations that override well-written tool descriptions, so reviewing the prompt is the first move when a tool starts winning selections it should lose. The escalation tool's description may also need work, but the prompt is what changed and what repeats the keyword. Narrow descriptions elsewhere would show up as a different failure. Temperature does not explain a consistent bias toward one tool.

choices.text: The escalate_to_human description, which is probably too broad and needs boundary conditions added.
The other tools' descriptions, which are probably too narrow to match the requests being escalated.
The system prompt itself, whose repeated escalation keywords are creating an unintended pull toward it.
The temperature setting, which may be high enough to make tool selection inconsistent between turns.

hints: Something changed just before the behaviour changed, and it repeats one word a lot.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

A customer asks about an order that does not exist. lookup_order returns isError with "no order found", and the agent retries three times before telling the customer the system is down. How should the tool respond to this case?
cards.answer: An access failure and a valid empty result are different things: this query executed and answered, so it is a success with zero rows and the agent should tell the customer no order matched. Marking it transient produces exactly the wasted retries described. Calling it a validation error implies the input was malformed when it was merely unmatched. Nothing suggests a permission problem.

choices.text: As a validation error, since the identifier the customer supplied did not correspond to a real order.
As a transient error with a retry delay, so the agent waits in case the record is still propagating.
As a successful call with an empty result, since the query ran correctly and found no match.
As a permission error, since the agent may simply lack access to the account that owns the order.

hints: The query ran and answered. Nothing failed.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your payment gateway occasionally times out for a few seconds. Today the MCP tool returns errorCategory: "transient" and isRetryable: true, and the agent retries immediately, forever, until the conversation is abandoned. What else does the error response need?
cards.answer: The structured metadata tells the agent what kind of failure occurred and whether another attempt could ever succeed; how many attempts to make, and when to give up, is a decision for the code running the loop. The category is accurate - a gateway timeout is transient. Flipping the flag to false would suppress retries that do succeed. A longer description does not bound a loop.

choices.text: A different category, because an error that cannot be retried indefinitely is not really transient.
A bounded retry policy in the calling code, since the flags describe the error, not the loop.
A longer human-readable description, so the agent can decide on its own how many attempts are reasonable.
isRetryable set to false, so the agent stops retrying and explains the outage to the customer instead.

hints: The metadata describes the failure. Ask who is supposed to decide how many times to try.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

You want to guarantee that every turn of the support agent produces a tool call rather than a conversational reply, because the orchestration layer downstream only knows how to consume tool results. You do not want to name which tool. Which setting fits?
cards.answer: "any" is the setting that guarantees the model calls a tool without dictating which one. "auto" permits a plain text response, which is the failure being avoided. Forcing the escalation tool turns every turn into an escalation. Passing a single tool guarantees a call but throws away the rest of the agent's capability.

choices.text: tool_choice set to "auto", which is the default and lets the model call a tool whenever one applies.
tool_choice set to "any", which requires a tool call while leaving the selection to the model.
tool_choice set to "any" with only one tool passed, which removes the ambiguity entirely.
tool_choice forced to escalate_to_human, which guarantees a call and covers the fallback case.

hints: You want a guaranteed call without naming the tool - that is exactly one of the three settings.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your .mcp.json contains "env": { "SUPPORT_API_TOKEN": "sk-live-4f2a..." } and the file is committed. An engineer proposes adding it to .gitignore. What should you do instead?
cards.answer: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json is the mechanism for exactly this: shared, version-controlled server configuration with the credential resolved at runtime. Gitignoring the file hides the configuration the team is supposed to receive. Moving to user scope loses the shared definition. Rotation limits damage without preventing it, and a second committed file still commits the secret.

choices.text: Split the file so the server lives in .mcp.json and the credentials live in a second committed file.
Move the whole server definition into each engineer's ~/.claude.json, which is never committed.
Replace the literal with ${SUPPORT_API_TOKEN} so the file stays in version control without the secret.
Keep the token in the file and rotate it on a schedule, so a leak has a limited useful lifetime.

hints: The file is supposed to be committed. Only the value inside it is not.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

A conversation covers three separate issues over forty turns. By the end, the agent confuses which order number belongs to which issue and quotes a refund amount from the wrong one. Summarization is already preserving the general narrative. What should you add?
cards.answer: Multi-issue sessions need structured issue data - order IDs, amounts, statuses - persisted in a separate context layer that survives summarization, because narrative summaries are exactly where those associations blur. Restating everything each turn floods the reply and still lives inside the summarized history. More budget delays the same loss. Splitting conversations breaks the shared customer context the agent needs.

choices.text: A structured per-issue context layer holding each issue's order ID, amount and status, kept outside the summary.
A larger summarization budget so the narrative retains more of the original wording for each issue.
A rule that the agent restates all three issues in full at the top of every one of its replies.
A separate conversation per issue, so no single context ever has to track more than one of them.

hints: The narrative survives; the association between issue and number is what dissolves.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your return policy covers price adjustments on your own site within 14 days. A customer asks you to match a competitor's lower price. The policy says nothing about competitors. What should the agent do?
cards.answer: Policy gaps are an explicit escalation trigger: the question is not whether the case is hard but whether the policy speaks to it. Declining invents a rule the policy does not state. Approving it stretches an adjacent rule into a decision nobody authorized. Collecting evidence does not resolve who is allowed to decide.

choices.text: Decline, because a request the policy does not cover is a request the company does not offer.
Approve it under the price adjustment rule, since a price match is a kind of price adjustment.
Escalate, because the policy is silent on this request rather than complex to apply.
Ask the customer to submit the competitor's listing, then decide once the evidence is available.

hints: The question is not whether the case is hard, but whether anyone has authorized an answer.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

A customer writes: "This is the third time I've had to chase this. Absolutely unacceptable." The issue itself is a standard damaged-item replacement the agent can process immediately. What is the right response?
cards.answer: Frustration is not the same as a request for a human, and the issue is within the agent's capability: acknowledge, resolve, and escalate only if the customer reiterates a preference for a person. Escalating on sentiment uses an unreliable proxy for case complexity. Ignoring the tone resolves the ticket and not the relationship. Offering a handoff first delays a resolution that is already available.

choices.text: Ask whether they would prefer to speak to a human before doing anything about the damaged item.
Process the replacement without commenting on the tone, since the resolution is what actually fixes the problem.
Escalate immediately, because the message shows the frustration threshold for a human handoff has been reached.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer the replacement now, escalating only if they still ask for a human.

hints: Being angry is not the same as asking for a person, and the fix is already within reach.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

The refund step of a multi-step resolution fails while the earlier steps succeeded: the customer was identified and the return was authorized. Your handler currently discards everything and reports "resolution failed". What should it report instead?
cards.answer: Structured error context including what was attempted and what partial results exist is what lets the next actor resume rather than restart. A generic failure message throws away the identification and authorization already done. Reporting success hides a refund that never happened. Discarding partial results forces the customer through steps that already succeeded.

choices.text: A generic failure with a suggestion that the customer try again later, keeping the message simple.
The failure type, the step that failed, and the partial results achieved, so recovery can resume.
Success, since two of the three steps completed and the customer's return is already authorized.
The failure only, since partial results from an incomplete workflow should not be relied on.

hints: Two of the three steps produced real results. Throwing them away costs the customer the work again.

cards.question:
**Scenario 1 - Customer Support Resolution Agent**

Your escalation criteria are written as clear rules, yet the agent still mishandles borderline cases: a customer who mentions a lawyer in passing, a policy that half-applies, a request that is partly covered. What addition most improves judgment on these?
cards.answer: Few-shot examples that demonstrate handling of ambiguous cases, including the reasoning for choosing one action over a plausible alternative, are what let the model generalize judgment to novel borderline situations. Enumerating observed cases only covers the ones already seen. "Escalate when unsure" relies on self-assessed uncertainty, which is poorly calibrated. Requiring an explanation documents the choice without improving it.

choices.text: A longer rule list that enumerates each borderline case observed in production so far.
Few-shot examples of ambiguous cases showing why one action was chosen over the plausible alternative.
A required reasoning paragraph before each decision, so the choice is at least explained.
An instruction to escalate whenever the agent is unsure which rule applies to the request.

hints: The rules are already clear; what is missing is worked examples of the cases that sit on the line.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Your repository has a root CLAUDE.md and a CLAUDE.md inside packages/api/. An engineer working in packages/api/ reports that the root conventions seem to apply too, and asks whether the nested file replaces them. What is the correct description of the hierarchy?
cards.answer: The configuration hierarchy is additive across user-level, project-level and directory-level files, so a package file adds its conventions on top of the project ones rather than shadowing them. Nearest-file-wins and root-only both describe a replacement that does not happen. File size plays no part in which configuration loads.

choices.text: Whichever file is larger applies, because Claude Code loads the most complete configuration it finds.
Only the root file applies, since directory-level CLAUDE.md files are read but not loaded into context.
Both apply: user, project and directory levels layer together rather than one replacing another.
Only the nearest file applies, so the directory-level file replaces the project-level one entirely.

hints: Ask whether the levels replace each other or stack on top of each other.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You split your monolithic CLAUDE.md by replacing long sections with @import lines pointing at files in docs/standards/. A teammate expects the session to start with far fewer tokens and is surprised it does not. Why?
cards.answer: @import keeps the configuration modular and gives each standard one source of truth, but the referenced content is pulled in at load time, so the context cost is unchanged. What does reduce context is path-scoped rules, which load only when a matching file is edited. The other explanations describe restrictions and caching behaviour that are not how imports work.

choices.text: Each @import adds its own overhead, which offsets most of the savings from splitting the file up.
The imports failed silently because @import only accepts paths inside the .claude/ directory.
Imported files are expanded when the configuration loads, so @import organizes content rather than deferring it.
Claude Code caches the previous version of CLAUDE.md until the session is restarted with a fresh cache.

hints: Modularity and context savings are two different benefits, and only one of them is what this mechanism gives you.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Two engineers on the same repository get different behaviour from Claude Code: one has the team's commit message format applied automatically, the other does not. Both are on the current main branch. What is the first thing to run?
cards.answer: /memory lists the memory files currently loaded and is the documented way to diagnose behaviour that differs between sessions - here it would show one engineer's rule living in user-level configuration. Checking git status assumes the difference is in tracked files, which /memory would establish first. /compact reduces context rather than reporting configuration. Re-cloning is a heavy step before the diagnosis exists.

choices.text: /memory, to compare which memory files each session actually has loaded.
A fresh clone on both machines, to eliminate any local difference in the working tree.
git status, to confirm neither engineer has uncommitted changes to the configuration files.
/compact, to rule out that one session lost the instruction during a context reduction.

hints: One command reports what configuration a session actually has loaded.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Your team's /migrate skill is invoked without arguments about half the time, and Claude then guesses a target version. You want developers to be prompted for the version when they invoke it bare. Which frontmatter field does that?
cards.answer: argument-hint exists to prompt developers for the parameters a skill expects when it is invoked without them. allowed-tools restricts the tool surface and says nothing about input. context: fork isolates the skill's context and would let a wrong guess run in isolation rather than prevent it. There is no required-arguments field in the frontmatter.

choices.text: context: fork, which isolates the skill so a wrong guess cannot affect the main session.
argument-hint, which tells the developer what parameter the skill expects.
allowed-tools, which constrains the skill until the required input is supplied.
A required-arguments list, which blocks execution until every argument has a value.

hints: The problem is a missing input at invocation time, and one frontmatter field exists for exactly that.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You are deciding between a skill and a CLAUDE.md section for two things: the repository's import ordering rule, which applies to every file, and a five-step release checklist run at the end of each sprint. Which placement is right?
cards.answer: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards and a skill is for an on-demand, task-specific workflow, which is exactly the split between a per-file rule and a sprint-end checklist. Reversing them loads a rare procedure into every session and makes a universal rule optional. Putting both in either place gets one of the two wrong.

choices.text: Import ordering in CLAUDE.md, release checklist in a skill.
Import ordering in a skill, release checklist in CLAUDE.md.
Both in CLAUDE.md, so neither depends on someone remembering to invoke it.
Both in skills, so the always-loaded configuration stays as small as it can be.

hints: One applies to every file, always. The other runs a few times a month.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Your Terraform lives under terraform/ and nowhere else, and its conventions are long. Your test files are spread across the whole tree. You want both sets of conventions applied automatically. What is the most maintainable pairing?
cards.answer: Conventions that follow a file type across the tree need a glob-scoped rule; conventions confined to one directory can use either mechanism, which is why the Terraform half has two acceptable answers. Directory files cannot follow tests spread across dozens of folders. One rule with both globs would load Terraform conventions while editing a test. Root sections rely on inference rather than matching.

choices.text: A directory-level CLAUDE.md for each, placed in terraform/ and in every directory containing tests.
One path-scoped rule listing both glob patterns, so a single file covers both sets of conventions.
A section in the root CLAUDE.md for each, relying on Claude to match the file being edited.
A path-scoped rule for the tests, and either a rule or a directory CLAUDE.md for Terraform.

hints: One convention follows a directory; the other follows a file type across the whole tree.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

A rule file in .claude/rules/ has frontmatter paths: ["src/api/**/*"], and engineers report the API conventions are not applied when they edit src/api/handlers/users.ts. The conventions themselves are correct. What should you inspect?
cards.answer: Path scoping depends on the file living in .claude/rules/ and carrying valid YAML frontmatter with a paths field, so a malformed header is what silently disables it. The pattern src/api/**/* does match nested files. Rules are not imported through CLAUDE.md. Path rules are evaluated against the file being edited, not fixed at session start.

choices.text: Whether the engineers restarted their sessions, since path rules are evaluated once when the session starts.
Whether the glob should be src/api/* instead, since ** only matches directories and not the files inside them.
Whether the rule file is listed in CLAUDE.md, since rules must be imported before their paths are evaluated.
Whether the file is in .claude/rules/ with valid YAML frontmatter, since a malformed header disables the scoping.

hints: The conventions are fine and the glob is fine. Look at the envelope around them.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

A ticket says: add a feature flag to gate a new checkout flow. There are three plausible places to put the flag, each with different rollout and testing implications, and the team has no precedent. The change itself touches four files. Which mode fits?
cards.answer: Plan mode is for tasks with multiple valid approaches and architectural implications, which is what "three plausible places with different rollout implications" describes - file count is not the criterion. Treating it as fully specified ignores that the decision itself is the open question. Splitting by file plans the easy part and improvises the rest.

choices.text: Plan mode for the first file and direct execution for the remaining three, once the pattern is set.
Plan mode, because several valid approaches exist and the choice has consequences beyond the edit.
Direct execution, because the requirement is fully specified and only the location is open.
Direct execution, because four files is a small change and plan mode is meant for large refactors.

hints: Count the open decisions, not the changed files.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You ask for a fix to three bugs in a date-handling module. Two of them are independent typos in unrelated functions; the third is a timezone bug whose fix changes the shape of the value the other two functions consume. How should you send the work?
cards.answer: Interacting problems belong in a single detailed message so the model can reconcile them; independent ones can be handled sequentially. Batching everything ignores the distinction, and so does the blanket one-per-message rule. Fixing the typos first locks in code the timezone change will have to revisit.

choices.text: All three in one message, since batching always reduces the number of round trips needed.
The two typos first, then the timezone bug, so the simple fixes are locked in before the risky one.
The timezone bug together with the two functions it affects in one message, since those fixes interact.
One bug per message in every case, since sequential iteration keeps each change reviewable.

hints: Two of the three fixes cannot affect each other. The third can.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You want Claude to implement a rate limiter that satisfies specific behaviour under burst traffic, at the boundary of the window, and when the clock jumps backwards. Prose descriptions of these cases have not produced a correct implementation. What approach works better?
cards.answer: Test-driven iteration - writing tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and performance first, then feeding the failures back - is the documented technique when a behaviour must be pinned down precisely. More prose is what already failed. Comparing three implementations still needs a way to judge them. Deferring the edge cases postpones the part that is actually hard.

choices.text: Write the test suite covering those cases first, then iterate by sharing the failures.
Implement the happy path first and add the edge cases as follow-up requests afterwards.
Ask for three implementations and keep whichever handles the edge cases best.
Write a longer specification that describes each of the three cases in more precise prose.

hints: You can describe the behaviour, or you can make it checkable. One of those has already failed.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You are three phases into a refactor. The first phase produced a detailed map of the module boundaries, and you are about to spawn subagents for phase two. What should you do with the phase-one findings?
cards.answer: Summarizing the findings of one exploration phase and injecting the summary into the next phase's agents is the documented way to carry understanding across a context boundary. Letting subagents rediscover it pays for the same exploration twice. The full transcript reintroduces the verbose output the summary exists to replace. Keeping it in the coordinator leaves the subagents doing their work blind.

choices.text: Store them in the coordinator only, since the coordinator is the agent that needs the map.
Pass the full phase-one transcript to each subagent so nothing is lost in summarization.
Rely on the subagents to rediscover what they need, since they will read the same code.
Summarize them and inject the summary into each subagent's initial context.

hints: The next agents start with nothing, and re-deriving the map costs what phase one already cost.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Halfway through a long session the context is dominated by file reads from an exploration you have finished with, and the next phase needs room. You want to keep working in the same session. What is the direct move?
cards.answer: /compact reduces context usage during extended exploration sessions when the window has filled with verbose discovery output, and it keeps the session going. Starting over is the fallback when the session must be abandoned, not the direct move. Instructing the model to forget does not remove tokens from the window. max_tokens caps a single response and does not reclaim context.

choices.text: Run /compact to condense the accumulated discovery output before the next phase begins.
Start a new session and paste in the parts of the transcript that still matter.
Reduce max_tokens so subsequent responses leave more of the window for the conversation.
Ask Claude to forget the earlier files, so they stop being considered in later reasoning.

hints: There is a command for exactly this, and it does not require leaving the session.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Your CI job concatenates twelve per-module analyses and asks for one consolidated migration plan. Modules two through ten are consistently underrepresented in the plan, while the first and last are always covered. What is the mechanism and the mitigation?
cards.answer: Models process the beginning and end of a long input reliably and may omit material from the middle, and the documented mitigation is to lead with a key-findings summary and structure the detail under explicit section headers. Nothing is being truncated - the middle is present and under-weighted. Reordering accepts the loss for whatever ends up in the middle. Response length is not what is dropping the content.

choices.text: The lost-in-the-middle effect; put a findings summary first and mark each module with an explicit header.
Alphabetical bias in aggregation; reorder the modules so the important ones lead the input.
Insufficient max_tokens on the response; raise it so the plan has room to mention every module.
Token truncation of the middle of the input; shorten each analysis until the whole request fits comfortably.

hints: The first and last are always fine. That is the tell.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Two weeks ago you ran a named session that analyzed a service in depth. Since then a large refactor landed and most of the files it read no longer look the same. You want that analysis today. What is the most reliable approach?
cards.answer: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming, because a resumed session reasons over cached results that no longer describe the code. Resuming as-is compounds the staleness. Resuming and re-reading everything pays the full exploration cost inside a polluted context. Forking branches from the same stale baseline.

choices.text: Resume the named session, since its conclusions are still the best starting point available.
Start a new session and inject a structured summary of the earlier conclusions as context.
Resume the named session and ask it to re-read every file it examined the first time.
Fork the old session, so the stale analysis stays intact while the new branch updates it.

hints: The conclusions are still worth having; the cached tool results describing the files are not.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

You have one session that has built a solid understanding of a legacy scheduler. You now want to try a queue-based redesign and an event-driven redesign, compare them, and keep the analysis you already paid for. Which mechanisms do you use, and in what order?
cards.answer: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline, so two forks give two clean explorations that both inherit the analysis. Resuming the same session alternately lets the designs contaminate each other in one history. A single fork resumed back and forth has the same problem. New sessions with a pasted summary work but discard the live analysis context that already exists.

choices.text: fork_session twice from the analysis session, exploring one redesign in each branch.
--resume the analysis session twice, once per redesign, in alternating turns.
Start both redesigns as new sessions and paste the analysis summary into each of them.
fork_session once, then --resume that fork whenever you switch between the two redesigns.

hints: Two clean branches, one shared starting point, and neither should see the other.

cards.question:
**Scenario 2 - Code Generation with Claude Code**

Your refactoring assistant reports every deviation from the style guide as an issue, and developers now skim past genuine logic errors buried among them. You still want style enforced somewhere. What is the most effective change to the prompt?
cards.answer: Explicit categorical criteria that name what to report and what to skip are what improve precision, and moving style into its own pass keeps it enforced without drowning the signal. Ranking still delivers the same noise below the fold. "Only high-confidence" is the vague confidence-based instruction that does not improve precision. Capping the count truncates a list that is still mostly noise.

choices.text: Cap the number of reported issues per file so the list stays short enough to read.
Ask for issues to be ranked by severity so the important ones appear at the top of the list.
Ask the assistant to report only issues it considers high-confidence and skip the rest.
State which categories to report and which to skip, and route style to a separate pass.

hints: Style still matters somewhere - just not mixed into the same list as logic errors.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

A user asks: "What is the current price of copper?" The coordinator spawns four search subagents, runs document analysis, synthesis and report generation, and answers ninety seconds later. Comparable queries behave the same way. What should change?
cards.answer: Deciding which subagents a query actually needs is the coordinator's job, and dynamic selection is what keeps a factual lookup from paying for a research pipeline. Shorter budgets keep every agent in the path and degrade each one's work. Asking the user offloads a routing decision the coordinator can make from the query. Skipping only the final step leaves most of the cost in place.

choices.text: The report generator should be skipped for one-line answers, leaving the rest of the pipeline intact.
The user interface should let the requester choose between a fast lookup and a full research run.
The pipeline should stay fixed, with each subagent given a shorter time budget for simple queries.
The coordinator should assess query complexity and invoke only the subagents that query needs.

hints: A one-line factual question is being charged the price of a research project. Someone should be deciding.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

Your coordinator prompt tells each search subagent exactly which three queries to run and in what order. Subagents that hit a dead end return empty rather than trying an adjacent phrasing. What should the coordinator's prompts specify instead?
cards.answer: Coordinator prompts should specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt when a line of enquiry fails. A longer prescribed list is the same rigidity with more entries. Retrying an identical query repeats a search that already returned nothing. Prescribing sources narrows adaptability further.

choices.text: A rule that an empty result must be retried with the same query before being reported.
The exact sources each subagent should consult, so dead ends become less likely in the first place.
The research goal and the quality criteria for a good result, leaving the method to the subagent.
A longer list of queries, so a subagent that exhausts the first three has more to fall back on.

hints: The prompts describe a procedure. Ask what they should describe instead so a dead end is survivable.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

The report subagent produces prose that mixes quarterly revenue figures, market news and technical benchmark results into uniform paragraphs. Readers say the financial data is unreadable. What should the subagent's output design specify?
cards.answer: Synthesis output should render different content types appropriately rather than converting everything to one uniform format, which is what makes financial data readable. Sectioning by source scatters a single topic across the report. Verbatim quoting preserves accuracy without fixing presentation. Generating two reports doubles the work and still has to choose a format for each.

choices.text: That the report is split into one section per source, so all of a given source's material stays together in one place.
That the report is generated twice, once optimized for readability and once for completeness.
That each content type is rendered in its own form: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as lists.
That numeric data is always quoted verbatim from the source rather than restated in the surrounding prose.

hints: Numbers, news and benchmarks do not read well in the same shape.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

You define your subagents with AgentDefinition entries. The document analysis agent occasionally issues web searches when a document reference is unclear, producing results the coordinator did not ask for. What is the cleanest correction?
cards.answer: Tool restrictions in the AgentDefinition keep each subagent inside its specialization, which is what prevents cross-role misuse structurally. A prompt instruction is probabilistic and the tool remains selectable. Discarding results afterwards pays for the wrong calls first. Priority between agents does not stop one from making a call it should not make.

choices.text: Give the web search agent a higher priority so the coordinator prefers its results over the other agent's.
Add a line to its system prompt telling it never to search the web under any circumstances.
Restrict that agent's tool set in its definition so web search is not available to it at all.
Let the coordinator discard any web results that arrive from the document analysis agent.

hints: The capability is available to an agent whose role does not include it.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

Your synthesis subagent receives findings as one long concatenated block of subagent prose. It produces coherent summaries but the coordinator cannot tell which claim came from which agent. What should the upstream agents return instead?
cards.answer: Structured output that separates content from metadata is what preserves attribution when context passes between agents, because the mapping travels with the claim. Prefixing an agent name identifies the author, not the source. Shorter prose loses the same attribution in fewer words. Detached source lists cannot be matched back to individual claims.

choices.text: The same prose, with the name of the contributing agent prefixed to each paragraph it wrote.
Prose plus a separate list of every source consulted during that agent's run.
Shorter prose, so the synthesis agent has fewer paragraphs to keep straight.
Structured findings that separate the claim from its metadata: source name, URL, excerpt and date.

hints: The claim and where it came from have to travel together, as data rather than as prose.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

A research request asks for a comparison across three technologies, three regions and two time periods. Your coordinator currently sends it to one search subagent as a single instruction, and the results are thin in most cells. What should it do first?
cards.answer: Multi-part requests should be decomposed into distinct items investigated in parallel against shared context, then synthesized into one answer. Sending an identical instruction to three agents produces three overlapping attempts at the same thing. Narrowing the question answers a smaller question than was asked. Repeating the same undecomposed run pays again for the same thin coverage.

choices.text: Send the same instruction to three subagents and merge whatever each of them returns.
Ask the requester to narrow the question to one technology before any research begins.
Decompose the request into distinct items and investigate them in parallel against shared context.
Run the single subagent repeatedly until the coverage of each cell stops improving.

hints: Eighteen cells were sent as one instruction to one agent.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

Your search subagent has search_web ("Searches the web") and search_archive ("Searches the archive"). It routinely sends historical queries to the web tool and current-events queries to the archive. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
cards.answer: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection, and these two say nothing that distinguishes coverage or time range, which is exactly what the misrouting turns on. A date parameter records an intention without informing the choice. Merging discards a real distinction between two backends. A prompt rule hard-codes a cutoff that the descriptions should express.

choices.text: Merge them into one search tool that routes internally based on the dates in the query.
Add a system prompt rule sending anything older than two years to the archive tool.
Rewrite both descriptions to state coverage, date range, expected inputs and when to prefer each one.
Add a date_range parameter to both tools so the agent has to state the period it is targeting.

hints: Neither description says anything about coverage or time range, which is exactly what the routing turns on.

cards.question:
**Scenario 3 - Multi-Agent Research System**

You are writing the description for a new verify_claim tool that the synthesis agent will use. Which content matters most for reliable selection?
cards.answer: Descriptions should carry input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundary explanations against similar tools, because that is what the model reads when choosing. Backend internals and latency do not inform selection. The response shape is returned to the caller and does not help decide whether to call. A cost warning discourages use without clarifying when use is right.

choices.text: The exact JSON shape of the response, so the agent knows how to parse what comes back.
A warning that the tool is expensive and should only be used when it is genuinely necessary.
Accepted input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it rather than a full search.
